source.title: Movements of the retinae of jumping spiders (Salticidae: Dendryphantinae) in response to visual stimuli

quote: using them a jumping spider can make the difficult distinction be- tween potential prey (flies, etc.) and potential mates (other jumping spiders) at distances of at least ten body lengths (5-10 cm.)
note: secondary through Land 1969b. The same paper: the spider watches a target face-on for 1 to 10 s before acting (Discussion) and jumps from 1 to 2 cm.

value: the posterior lateral eyes detect movement and trigger a whole-body turn of the right size, made without visual feedback, which brings the target to the principal eyes
method: unpublished experiments reported in the discussion; see Land 1971 for the test

source.title: Movements of the retinae of jumping spiders (Salticidae: Dendryphantinae) in response to visual stimuli

quote: when a stimulus is seen by these eyes it evokes a series of leg movements which bring the animal's whole body round to face the stimulus, which is then picked up by the antero- median retinae

value: the side eyes respond only to movement: a target in view the whole time evokes turns only when it moves, and a light that only goes on and off evokes none
method: behavioural: spider holding a card ring, target on a rotating drum

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

where: Results, Turns made under open-loop conditions
quote: the system behaves as though it were completely blind to stationary objects.
note: 'Stimuli which change in intensity without moving (i.e. go on and off) have not been found to elicit turning' (Results, The adequate stimulus). 85 individuals of M. harfordi and M. aeneolus.

value: minimum target: lines narrower than 0.4 degrees never evoke turns; half-maximal response at about 0.7 degrees, just under the posterior lateral eyes' receptor spacing of about 1 degree; a 1 degree movement suffices
method: behavioural: turn probability against line width, stimuli 45 to 180 degrees from the axis

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

quote: To be seen, a stimulus must subtend more than 0-7° (slightly less than the distance between receptors) and must move through a minimum angle of about i°.
note: OCR 'i°' is 1°. Target speeds that evoke turns run from about 1 to 100 degrees/s (preliminary). A complex outline does not raise the chance of a turn; a moving hand or car serves as well as a fly.

value: latency: shortest 80 to 120 ms from the start of target movement; most turns begin within 100 ms of the target stopping; some come up to 1 s later and are still accurate, so the target's position is held for at least a second

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

quote: The shortest time observed between the beginning of movement of the target and the beginning of a turn was between 80 and 120 ms
note: the target moved for 200 ms. Turns run at 164 to 1120 degrees/s on average, up to 1775 degrees/s frame to frame, and last under 0.1 to 1.6 s.

value: open-loop turns: complete turns are aimed without visual feedback, mean error -0.5 degrees and standard deviation 16.2, so 50% land within 11 degrees of the target and 90% within 27; partial turns of 10 to 20 degrees also occur; turns are as accurate in darkness

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

quote: For this animal, which was typical of six others examined, the mean error for all turns was —0-5°, which is negligible, and the standard deviation i6•2°.
note: OCR 'i6•2' is 16.2. The principal eyes, moving, can reach targets up to 35 degrees either side of the midline, so nearly every complete turn delivers the target to them.

value: response probability depends on where the target is: highest at about 40 to 90 degrees from the front, low behind and low straight ahead (where the principal eyes move instead)

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

quote: The probability of a turn being made is greatest for stimuli 40-900 from the spider's front, and decreases to a low value for stimuli behind the animal, and immedi- ately in front of it.
note: OCR '40-900' is 40-90°. Even an optimal target evokes a turn only some of the time (a maximum near 15% in one test): a central veto, since the same movements often evoke principal-eye saccades without a turn.

value: habituation is tied to retinal location: repeated movement at one place stops evoking turns within one or two movements (at most 15), while a target moved to a fresh place a few degrees away is answered again; touch restores responsiveness

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

quote: turns can still be evoked by moving the stimulus a few degrees to a previously unstimulated part of the retina.
note: full recovery takes hours. This location-specific habituation is a measured counterpart to the gaze's 'avoid the last place' rule.

value: one anterior lateral eye: from 45 degrees on its own side across the midline to 15 degrees on the other side; overlap with the posterior lateral eye's field only at 40 to 45 degrees; one posterior lateral eye covers about 50 to 170 degrees on its side
method: behavioural: turns with single eyes covered with wax

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

where: Results, Fields of view of the lateral eyes
quote: The remaining left antero-lateral eye thus had a field of view from 45° left across the midline to 150 right
note: OCR '150' is 15°. Blinding the left PLE abolished responses at 170 to 50 degrees left. No responses at all with only the tiny posterior median eyes open.

value: the posterior median eyes are minute and probably vestigial; with only they uncovered, no turns were made

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

quote: Orientational turns of the kind that concern us here are thus mediated by the four lateral eyes (the postero-medial eyes are minute and probably vestigial)
note: tested in Metaphidippus; 'No responses of any kind were produced when only the tiny postero-median eyes remained open.'

value: beside turning to face, moving things seen by the side eyes make the spider duck under its leaf, or, when chased, keep the pursuer directly behind it

source.title: Orientation by jumping spiders in the absence of visual feedback

where: Results, Other responses mediated by the lateral eyes
quote: When a spider is being chased by, for example, a biologist's pencil, it con- tinuously adjusts its track so as to keep the stimulus directly behind.

method: anatomical, with the telephoto system's focal length

source.title: The principal eyes of a jumping spider have a telephoto component

quote: form an hexagonal array with a minimum receptor- row spacing of 1.4 J..Lm (ref. 8), corresponding to a visual angle of 2.4 arc min.
note: 2.4 arcmin = 0.04 degrees, so 1/(2 x 0.04) = 12.5 cycles/degree; OCR 'J..Lm' is µm. The same page gives 0.12 mm resolved at 20 cm.

method: anatomical: Nyquist limit of the layer 1 mosaic

source.title: The principal eyes of a jumping spider have a telephoto component

quote: The highest spatial frequency that can be recon- structed by layer 1 with minimum receptor-row spacing 1.4 J..Lm and distance 1,980 J..Lm from the posterior nodal point of the telephoto system is 1,980/2.8 = 710 rad- 1.
note: 710 cycles per radian / 57.3 = 12.4 cycles/degree. The optics pass up to 760 per radian (13.3 cycles/degree), so the mosaic is well matched to the lens; without the pit the retina could reconstruct only 420 per radian (7.3 cycles/degree).

value: telephoto camera eye: a diverging pit lens (radius about 5 µm, power about -12,800 dioptres) behind the corneal lens magnifies the image 1.54 times

source.title: The principal eyes of a jumping spider have a telephoto component

quote: the magnification achieved by the pit lens is 1.54 (see Fig. 3)
note: the corneal lens has a graded refractive index that corrects spherical aberration, so the eye is probably diffraction limited (p. 580). The pit's curvature varies among species and is negligible in some (p. 579).

source.title: The principal eyes of a jumping spider have a telephoto component

quote: About 100 receptors in the centre of layer 1 lie behind the curved region of the pit ... In total they have a field of view of 0.6°.
note: the whole retina is 250 µm high and 25 µm wide; its upper and lower arms extend the vertical field at lower magnification and with blurred focus.

value: layer 1's staircase of receptor tips (25 µm from side to side) gives best images of objects 15 to 29 cm away and a total depth of field from 9 cm to infinity; no accommodation

source.title: The principal eyes of a jumping spider have a telephoto component

quote: the distal ends of those of layer 1 (Fig. 2) receive best images from objects 15-29 em in front of the spider and have a total depth of field of 9 em to oo.
note: OCR 'em' is cm and 'oo' is infinity.

method: this sheet's arithmetic: 1980 µm (posterior nodal distance of the telephoto system) / 350 µm aperture

source.title: The principal eyes of a jumping spider have a telephoto component

quote: The limiting aperture is a ring of pigment, 350 J..Lm in diameter and 315 J..Lm behind the corneal surface.
note: an estimate from two figures on the page; the paper does not state an F-number.

value: some jumping spiders, Portia fimbriata among them, tell conspecifics from prey at 15 to 20 cm; Trite planiceps at 20 cm
method: as cited (Forster 1979; Jackson and Blest, then in preparation)

source.title: The principal eyes of a jumping spider have a telephoto component

quote: Some salti- cids, including P. fimbriata, seem to discriminate between conspecifics and prey at distances of 15-20 em (refs 12, 13)
note: secondary through Williams and McIntyre 1980.

source.title: Spectral sensitivities of jumping spider eyes

quote: The anterior and posterior lateral eyes have a single type of visual cell with a maximum spectral sensitivity at about 535-540 nm.
note: chromatic adaptation did not change the curve. The species is Menemerus confusus (the paper's name), not M. confluens. The journal pages are 29-41 as printed on the paper.

source.title: Spectral sensitivities of jumping spider eyes

where: Results, Anterior and Posterior Lateral Eyes
quote: Each curve has a single peak at 535-540 nm and a dip at the near ultraviolet region.

method: intracellular recording of 7 cells and ERG with chromatic adaptation

source.title: Spectral sensitivities of jumping spider eyes

quote: The anterior median eye has four types of visual cells with maximum sensitivities at about 360, 480-500, 520 540 and 580 nm, respectively.
note: seven cells only: one at 360, two at 480-500, three at 520-540, one at 580 nm (Addendum). Blest et al. 1981 found only UV and green in Plexippus and warned that yellow pigment granules may have entered the light path. Treat as unconfirmed.

source.title: Spectral sensitivities of jumping spider eyes

quote: We observed one UV cell (peak sensitivity is 360 nm), two blue cells (480-500 nm), three green cells (520-540 nm) and one yellow cell (580 nm)
note: a single cell; contested by Blest et al. 1981.

source.title: Spectral sensitivities of jumping spider eyes

quote: We observed one UV cell (peak sensitivity is 360 nm), two blue cells (480-500 nm), three green cells (520-540 nm) and one yellow cell (580 nm)

value: broad ERG sensitivity from 490 to 590 nm with a further peak near 365 nm

source.title: Spectral sensitivities of jumping spider eyes

quote: In the visible light region, the curves have a very broad peak between 490 nm and 590 nm, and several, smaller peaks at 490-500 nm, 520-540 nm and/or 580 nm.
note: orange adaptation depressed long-wavelength sensitivity and blue adaptation short; responses from the back of the retina were affected most by long wavelengths.
